justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 79.05 is essentially anchored to the current price level, assuming no major overnight catalysts and mean-reversion tendencies that keep short-term moves contained. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 79.20 reflects a mild positive bias, perhaps driven by prevailing momentum or a constructive macro backdrop at the time of the forecast. The one-month estimate of 79.80 extrapolates that gradual drift further, consistent with a base case where fundamentals remain broadly supportive and no significant shocks materialize. In all three cases, the point estimates are not expressing a strong directional conviction but rather a continuation of existing trends with a small positive lean.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the well-established principle that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.1 units, capturing normal intraday and overnight volatility. By one week, that range opens to nearly 5.8 units, incorporating the possibility of scheduled economic data releases, central bank commentary, or geopolitical developments that could shift sentiment meaningfully. At one month, the interval stretches to approximately 11.5 units, acknowledging that over a four-week window, a much broader set of macro and idiosyncratic factors can come into play, including earnings cycles, policy shifts, and changes in risk appetite.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in economic data — such as a sharp miss on employment figures or inflation coming in hotter than expected — could trigger a repricing that breaks below the lower bounds, particularly at the weekly and monthly horizons. Liquidity shocks or sudden risk-off episodes driven by geopolitical escalation could also produce moves well beyond what the intervals anticipate. On the upside, a dovish policy pivot, stronger-than-expected growth data, or a resolution of an existing geopolitical uncertainty could produce a rally that exceeds the upper bounds, especially over the monthly horizon where positive catalysts have more time to accumulate.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are probabilistic rather than absolute bounds, meaning by construction there is a 10% chance of outcomes falling outside them. Fat-tailed distributions in financial markets mean the true probability of extreme outcomes may be somewhat higher than a normal distribution would suggest. Correlation breaks — where assets that typically hedge each other move in the same direction — and model misspecification around regime changes represent structural sources of error that are difficult to quantify in advance but can render even well-constructed intervals too narrow in practice.
